proposals.name: Punchline precedes metadata; reads as performed line not reply
proposals.instruction: Score the ordering of joke text versus tweet metadata (the @midnight handle and the contest hashtag). 10 = the comedic content is the first thing on the line and the handle/hashtag are trailing metadata, so the line reads as a standalone performed utterance a reader encounters cold. 5 = metadata is interleaved mid-line or split around the joke. 0 = the tweet opens with '@midnight' and/or the contest hashtag before any comedic content, so the first thing read is an address to the show and the joke arrives as an afterthought appended to a reply. Judge only surface order, not joke quality.
proposals.rationale: This ordering separates the two halves almost cleanly. Every high-dense row here front-loads the joke -- R26 'We won't do Metric!' first, R52 'We Were Always Great' first, R44 'Git er done' first, R55 'Up the Holler' first -- while the card-favored rows overwhelmingly open on the handle: R03, R12, R04, R53, R19, R37 all begin '@midnight'. A scorecard scoring the joke text in isolation strips this off and cannot see it; a dense reader reading the raw string experiences the reply-prefixed versions as addressed-at-the-show rather than delivered, which flattens the timing.

proposals.name: Self-contained text; no link, image dependency, or piggyback hashtags
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entire joke is present in the text a reader can see. 10 = no URL, no attached-media reference, no hashtags beyond the single contest hashtag, and nothing whose meaning depends on something the reader would have to click or open. 3 = extra unrelated hashtags are stapled on for reach but the joke still resolves in text. 0 = the tweet carries a t.co link or clearly points at an image/video such that the text alone is an incomplete setup, or is stuffed with additional promotional hashtags. Do not reward or penalize the joke itself, only its self-sufficiency.
proposals.rationale: Every link-bearing or hashtag-stuffed row in this slice sits at the extreme low end of dense and comfortably above the middle on card: R18 (dense .010, t.co link), R10 (dense .022, t.co link), R48 (dense .025, link plus '#NeverForget'), R08 (dense .042, '#PointsMe #July4thBirthday'), R54 (dense .049, link), R60 (dense .223, '#STLCards'). That is six of the bottom rows sharing one surface property. A criterion bank built from joke-text features scores the residual phrase and never docks the dependency; a dense reader sees a joke whose payload is missing.

proposals.name: Spoken in character versus catalogued from outside
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry is phrased as an utterance the prompt's subject would actually produce, or as an observer's description of that subject. 10 = the line is in the subject's own mouth -- a thing said, a phrase in their idiom, a first-person or second-person address -- so the entry performs the category rather than reporting it. 5 = a noun phrase that a member of the group might plausibly say aloud but reads neutrally. 0 = a detached third-party inventory item, an anthropological label applied from outside, phrased the way a list-maker rather than a speaker would phrase it.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high redneck rows are almost all ventriloquism: R11 'Tell you what.', R24 'Y'all watch this', R44 'Git er done', R47 'That's my uncledad!', R05 'Science is bullsh*t!'. The card-high redneck rows are almost all outside inventory: R04 'multiple COPS appearances', R18 'automotive lawn art', R35 'barbecue flavored beard', R15 'WalMart special occasion'. Both halves are topically on-target, so a topic-fit criterion cannot separate them; the difference is who is speaking. This is the single most legible axis of disagreement in the slice.

proposals.name: Every word earns its slot under the word budget
proposals.instruction: Given the count the hashtag imposes (three, four, five words), score word economy jointly with count compliance. 10 = the count is met exactly and every single token is a content word doing comedic work, with no articles, prepositions, connectives, or filler quantifiers spending a slot. 5 = the count is met but one or two tokens are grammatical glue. 0 = the count is blown, or a large share of the tokens are structural filler or self-explanation rather than joke material.
proposals.rationale: Scarcity is the whole game in a fixed-word prompt, and the dense-high entries treat every slot as expensive: R36 'Moonshine, Overalls, Pickups' and R58 'Guns Nascar Beer Oligarchy' are pure content, no glue. The card-high entries spend slots freely: R27 'Tweeted from the wrong account' burns two on 'from the', R13 '16 Angry Men (and one woman)' spends its overflow explaining itself, R42 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?' is mostly transcription. A scorecard that checks 'is it funny' and 'does it fit the theme' passes all of these; density-per-token is invisible to it.

proposals.name: Discovered wordplay versus obvious substitution template
proposals.instruction: Score the generative mechanism of any wordplay. 10 = the wordplay is a discovery -- a coincidence in the language the author found, or a coinage that names a real thing that had no name -- such that a reader feels the author saw something. 5 = a competent pun with a small element of surprise. 0 = the joke is the output of a mechanical template a reader could run themselves: take a well-known title, swap in a topical noun, done, with the surprise lying entirely in the swap being legal rather than in it being apt. Score the mechanism, not whether you laughed.
proposals.rationale: This explains why the dense model is not simply anti-wordplay. It rates coinages highly -- R25 'Dog: My Copilot', R47 'That's my uncledad!', R09 'bruncle' -- while sitting far below the card on template swaps: R12 'Kill Bill of Rights', R34 'Judge Dread', R40 'Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz', R57 'Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda', R38 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation'. A criterion bank almost certainly rewards 'contains wordplay' as a positive, which over-credits exactly the template family, because template puns are the most legible and most checkable form of wordplay on the page.

proposals.name: Zero-lookup reference breadth
proposals.instruction: Score how much external knowledge the reader must already hold for the line to land, and how fast that retrieval is. 10 = every referent is common cultural furniture retrievable instantly by a general audience, so the joke fires on first read with no pause. 5 = one referent is moderately well known and a sizeable minority of readers would miss it. 0 = the joke turns on a name, show, fandom, era, or in-group marker that most readers would have to look up or would simply not recognize, so the line reads as inert to them.
proposals.rationale: The deepest card-over-dense rows are gated behind narrow referents: R10 'David Brent' (dense .022, a UK-only character), R48 'Drunk Shriners' (dense .025), R42 'Baby Jane' (dense .132, a 1962 film), R60 '#STLCards' (dense .223, requires a rivalry read). Against these, the dense-high rows lean on universally held material -- R44 'Git er done', R33 'Deep-fried Chocolate-covered Hostess Twinkie', R32 'Pass the ammunition'. A judge scoring 'is this a clever reference' rewards obscurity, since obscure references look more effortful; a reader scoring reach penalizes it.

proposals.name: Dark material owned from inside versus cruelty aimed from outside
proposals.instruction: For entries with taboo, dark, or offensive content, score the stance jointly with the transgression. 10 = the line commits fully to dark material and does so from a position of ownership or self-implication -- the speaker is inside the world being joked about, so the edge reads as bravado or confession. 5 = dark content delivered from a neutral vantage. 0 = the dark content is aimed downward at the subject as an accusation from a safe outside position, or leans on a genuinely victimizing image for shock with no voice behind it. Score stance and commitment; do not simply score how offensive the content is.
proposals.rationale: Transgression per se does not separate these halves, so stance must be doing the work. Owned-from-inside dark lines run high on dense: R07 'Meth, Meth, Meth', R01 'First Cousin lovin'', R47 'uncledad', R50 'ACTUAL Sister Wives', R05 'Science is bullsh*t!'. Externally aimed or victim-facing dark lines run high on card and low on dense: R19 'Family reunion Rohypnol' (dense .164, card .990 -- the widest gap in the slice) and R28 'Post sex grits' (dense .294, card .819). A shock-value or edginess criterion would score R19 at the top, which is precisely the over-credit.

proposals.name: Line scans as spoken comedy
proposals.instruction: Read the entry aloud and score its prosody. 10 = the line has audible comedic rhythm -- a stress pattern that lands, a triple beat, alliteration or assonance, a hard consonant or stressed syllable at the end so the line closes rather than trails. 5 = neutral phrasing, neither musical nor awkward. 0 = the line reads as flat prose or a database field, with unstressed trailing syllables, awkward stress collisions, or a shape no one would say out loud. Judge sound only; ignore meaning.
proposals.rationale: The top of the dense distribution is conspicuously percussive: R07 'Meth, Meth, Meth' is a triple beat, R36 'Moonshine, Overalls, Pickups' is a falling three-item cadence, R49 'Meth'd up Mondays' alliterates, R55 'Up the Holler' and R32 'Pass the ammunition' both close on stress. The card-favored entries are prose-shaped: R42 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?', R13 '16 Angry Men (and one woman)', R38 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation'. This is a delivery property that lives in the sound of the string and is invisible to any criterion phrased in terms of content.

proposals.name: Grammatical completion of the prompt frame
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry substitutes cleanly into the frame the hashtag sets up -- what a redneck says or is, what America is, what a scary story is. 10 = the line is a well-formed completion that could stand where the frame expects it, so the prompt and the entry lock together grammatically as well as topically. 5 = it fits with a small charitable reading. 0 = it is a loosely associated noun phrase or fragment dropped near the topic that does not actually complete the frame, so the reader supplies the connection themselves.
proposals.rationale: R30 'Need To Get Out', R52 'We Were Always Great' and R26 'We won't do Metric!' are all clean completions of 'America, in four words' -- each is a thing America would say or is. The card-favored side often supplies orbiting nouns instead: R18 'automotive lawn art' and R35 'barbecue flavored beard' are objects associated with the topic rather than answers to it, and R08 'Twerking Ever Since 2013' answers a different question than the one asked. A topical-relevance criterion scores association, which is why it passes the orbiting nouns; frame fit is stricter.

proposals.name: Specific recognized truth versus generic category token
proposals.instruction: Score observational validity at the level of specificity. 10 = the line names something the reader recognizes as actually and particularly true of the subject, at a grain fine enough that recognition feels earned -- the reader thinks 'that is exactly right' rather than 'yes, that is on the list'. 5 = accurate but broad. 0 = the entry deploys the most generic available token for the category, an item any reader could have named in one second as a stereotype placeholder, contributing recognition of the category but no observation about it.
proposals.rationale: R26 'We won't do Metric!' and R46 'How Free Are You?' and R25 'Dog: My Copilot' and R33 'Deep-fried Chocolate-covered Hostess Twinkie' are all specific enough that the observation is the joke. The card-favored side reaches for placeholders: R15 'WalMart special occasion', R04 'multiple COPS appearances', R53 'what's a dentist' -- each is the first stereotype token a person would produce, correct but uninformative. A theme-fit or on-topic criterion scores placeholders at the maximum, because a placeholder is by construction maximally on theme. This is a direct over-credit mechanism.

proposals.name: Non-obvious source choice given the prompt
proposals.instruction: Estimate how many independent entrants would land on this exact source, angle, or pivot word. 10 = the choice is one almost no one else would reach for, yet fits once seen. 5 = a moderately popular lane. 0 = the single most obvious source the prompt suggests, such that a room of entrants would produce near-duplicates of this line; the entry's only distinguishing move is one everyone else also made. Judge the freshness of the choice, not the execution.
proposals.rationale: The slice contains its own duplicate evidence. R13 '16 Angry Men (and one woman)' and R56 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders' are two riffs on the same source, both card-high and both dense-low; R22 'Star Wars VII: series finale' and R41 'Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie' are two riffs on another, again both card-high and dense-low. Convergence on the obvious source is exactly what a per-item scorecard cannot see, since it evaluates each item alone and each of these looks competently made. The dense-high rows -- R26, R39 -- take angles nothing in the prompt suggests.

proposals.name: Implied scene per word spent
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio of implied narrative to words on the page. 10 = a very short line detonates a whole scene, backstory, or consequence in the reader's head that the text never states, so the reader does most of the work and enjoys doing it. 5 = the line implies a little beyond its literal content. 0 = the line states its entire content explicitly with nothing left to infer, or is so long that whatever it implies is not a bargain for the reading cost.
proposals.rationale: R24 'Y'all watch this' is three words that summon an entire impending disaster, and R11 'Tell you what.' summons a whole speaker; R39 'But we're we really?' and R52 'We Were Always Great' each open a national argument in four words. Against these, R08 'Twerking Ever Since 2013 #PointsMe #July4thBirthday' and R59 'Me sleeping picture, live alone' spend more and imply less. A scorecard can readily check that a joke is present but has no natural way to price the inference the reader is invited to perform against the words spent buying it.

proposals.name: Authorial contribution relative to borrowed scaffold
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the laugh belongs to the author rather than to the recognizability of borrowed material. 10 = the memorable part of the line is the author's own invention -- a coinage, an original phrase, a construction that did not exist before -- even if a familiar frame is present. 5 = borrowed frame with a substantive original turn. 0 = the line is overwhelmingly a quoted title, slogan, or catchphrase with a minimal edit, so the reader's pleasure is mostly the pleasure of recognizing the source and the author supplied one word.
proposals.rationale: R42 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?' and R56 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders' and R14 'Tastes great, less filling' are mostly transcription with a light edit, and all three sit far higher on card than on dense. The dense-high side manufactures its own material: R09 coins 'bruncle', R47 coins 'uncledad', R49 coins 'Meth'd up Mondays'. Recognizability reads to a criterion judge as cleverness and to a reader as borrowed, which is a clean account of the over-credit direction here.

proposals.name: No structural scaffolding propping up the joke
proposals.instruction: Score whether the joke stands without construction apparatus. 10 = a single uninterrupted phrase; no colon-delimited setup-and-tagline, no sequel numbering, no parenthetical gloss, no appended explanation of the mechanism. 5 = one such device present but the joke would survive without it. 0 = the entry requires its scaffolding -- a parenthetical that explains the substitution, a colon that separates the borrowed title from the topical tag, a sequel number doing the work of a premise -- so the reader watches the machinery assemble the joke instead of receiving it.
proposals.rationale: Nearly every scaffolded entry in the slice is card-high and dense-low: R13 '(and one woman)' annotates its own swap, R38 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation' stacks a sequel number and a colon tag, R22 'Star Wars VII: series finale', R40 'Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz' and R56 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders' all use the colon to bolt the topical half onto the borrowed half. A criterion judge reads visible construction as craft; a reader reads it as the joke needing help to stand up.

proposals.name: Unrequested barb: real-world sting the prompt did not demand
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry smuggles a genuine political or cultural argument into a prompt that did not ask for one, and lands it in the prompt's own terms. 10 = the hashtag is nominally apolitical and the entry nonetheless delivers a real barb with a target and a point of view, so it works both as an answer and as a jab. 5 = mild editorial coloring. 0 = no argument beyond the prompt's literal ask, or the prompt already mandated the target so no risk was taken by aiming at it. Judge whether a stance was volunteered, not whether you agree with it.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high rows repeatedly convert a joke prompt into a claim: R16 'Proud Republican Tools', R21 'Democrats America's Retarded People', R23 'Guns, God, Government Corruption', R31 'Guns, No Abortions', R43 'Half will vote Trump.', R58 'Guns Nascar Beer Oligarchy' -- none of #Redneck_In_3_Words or #America_In_4_Words asks for politics. Meanwhile the card-high #GOPMovies rows such as R34 'Judge Dread' and R03 'All the White Moves' aim at a target the prompt already handed them, which is safe rather than sharp. A scorecard rewarding topical or political content scores both identically and so over-credits the mandated case.

proposals.name: Metadata-first layout: handle and hashtag before any content
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which tweet metadata precedes comedic content in the raw string. 10 = the tweet opens with '@midnight' and/or the contest hashtag, with all joke text after them. 5 = metadata is split around the content or sits mid-string. 0 = the joke text occupies the head of the string and all metadata trails at the end. Count only token order in the raw text. Do NOT judge whether either layout is better, funnier, or more professional; you are recording a layout habit, not evaluating it.
proposals.rationale: Reply-composed and standalone-composed entries split the slice: R02, R04, R06, R11, R22, R24, R56 and R57 all lead with '@midnight', while R01, R05, R09, R21 and R60 lead with the joke. The compose route is an interface accident -- whether the entrant was watching the show's timeline and hit reply, or wrote the line first -- and it cannot make the joke better or worse. But it deterministically changes what the first tokens of the string are, so any text-only model will pick it up, and it is dense enough in this slice to carry real predictive weight on its own.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's composition route -- tapping reply on the show's prompt tweet (which auto-inserts the handle first) versus composing a standalone tweet and appending tags

proposals.name: External link or attached-media dependency
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which the text points outside itself to a URL or attached media. 10 = a t.co or http link is present and the surrounding text reads as a caption for something not shown. 5 = a link is present but the text also reads as complete on its own. 0 = no link, no reference to an image, video, or anything to be opened. Record presence and apparent dependency only. Do NOT judge whether linking is appropriate, lazy, or effortful, and do not speculate about what the media contains.
proposals.rationale: R28, R37, R50 and R55 all carry links. Whether an entrant had a usable image on hand is upstream of the text and largely a matter of workflow and source access, not comic ability, so the fingerprint is a nuisance. I tag it mixed because the parent is not purely nuisance: an entrant who built a visual entry may have made a genuinely stronger contest submission, and a text-only readout systematically cannot see that half. Discounting this channel should therefore be reported with a sensitivity band, not as a clean correction.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's media-first workflow and access to an image or clip worth attaching (equipment, source material, and the habit of building visual entries)

proposals.name: Off-contest hashtag stuffing and points solicitation
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT of hashtags beyond the single contest hashtag. 10 = two or more additional hashtags unrelated to answering the prompt, including tags that solicit attention from the show or attach the entry to a separate trend. 5 = exactly one extra hashtag. 0 = the contest hashtag only. Count tags; do NOT judge whether the extra tags are witty, well chosen, annoying, or spammy, and do not let the joke's quality influence the count.
proposals.rationale: R41 carries '#PointsMe' and '#July4thBirthday', R28 carries '#NeverForget', and R29 carries '#STLCards'. These are reach mechanics: '#PointsMe' is a naked request aimed at the show, and the others bolt the entry onto unrelated trends. None of this changes how good the line is as an answer to the prompt, but all of it is highly visible in the string and covaries with a distinct population of entrants who tweet for reach. That is precisely the shape of a declared nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's audience-growth strategy -- follower-seeking, trend-piggybacking, and explicit bids for the show's attention

proposals.name: Self-annotating gloss that explains the joke's mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which the text explains its own construction. 10 = an explicit parenthetical or appended note spells out the substitution, the pun, or what the reader is supposed to notice. 5 = a mild clarifying aside. 0 = the line is delivered with no commentary on itself. Record only the presence and size of the self-explanation. Do NOT judge whether the explanation was needed, whether it helps, or whether the underlying joke is good.
proposals.rationale: R53 appends '(brother + uncle)' after 'bruncle' and R31 appends '(and one woman)' after '16 Angry Men'. Glossing is a behavioural tell of an entrant unsure the room will follow, which is upstream of the text and correlated with practice rather than with the merit of any single line. It is mixed rather than pure nuisance because reps in a format plausibly also improve the entries an author produces, so the parent has a real quality path as well as a spurious one, and the two rows here sit on opposite sides of the disagreement.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's inexperience with this format and its audience -- entrants with few reps hedge against not being understood by annotating

proposals.name: Show-directed and platform-meta content rather than prompt content
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which the text is about the show, the contest, Twitter mechanics, or the author's own account, rather than about the subject the prompt names. 10 = the entry's whole content is meta -- the show, being on the show, tweeting, one's own timeline. 5 = a meta element sits alongside a substantive answer. 0 = nothing meta; the line answers the prompt's subject only. Record subject matter only. Do NOT judge whether the meta angle is clever or cheap.
proposals.rationale: R50 is a quoted line about seeing oneself on the show, R49 is about tweeting from the wrong account, and R41 tags '#PointsMe' directly at the show. Venue-flattery and platform-meta are an audience-directed strategy: they are aimed at the receiving side rather than at the prompt, and their frequency tracks how invested an entrant is in the show's economy, not how funny the line is. The fingerprint is fully visible in the text, so it can bias a text-only model.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's fan relationship to the programme and the wish to be read out on air, which pulls entries toward flattering or referencing the venue

proposals.name: Ordinal or sequel escalation over an already-obvious source
proposals.instruction: MODE 3, position fingerprint. Score the EXTENT to which the text reads as a bid placed on top of a source someone else would obviously have claimed first: a number bumped one step past the canonical title, a sequel number, a colon-appended follow-on, or a 'part two' framing of a reference whose plain form is the first thing anyone would reach for. 10 = the entry only makes sense as an escalation of an already-taken obvious take. 5 = a familiar source used with a modest twist. 0 = no escalation structure; the source is either fresh or used plainly. You cannot see the entry's actual position in the stream -- score only the textual tell. Do NOT judge whether escalating was a good move.
proposals.rationale: The slice contains the escalation pattern in the open. R32 uses '12 Angry Men' plainly while R31 bids '16 Angry Men (and one woman)' -- an ordinal bump that only makes sense if twelve was gone. R54 'Speed 2:' and R17 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3:' both reach for a sequel number rather than the base title, and R39 'Star Wars VII: series finale' and R52 'Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie.' are two bids on one source. Arrival order is unobservable and has nothing to do with comic skill, but it leaves this legible trace. I tag it mixed because late arrival also forces genuine originality, so the parent has a real quality path too.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of the entry in the contest's stream of submissions -- how many other entries the author had already scrolled past before writing

proposals.name: News-cycle datedness markers pinning the entry to a moment
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT to which the text is anchored to a specific short-lived moment: a year, a named figure prominent only in a particular season, a current release, a sporting event in progress. 10 = the line cannot be read without knowing what was in the news that week. 5 = one moderately time-bound referent. 0 = nothing that dates the entry; the referents are durable. Record time-anchoring only. Do NOT judge whether topicality is desirable here, and do not penalise or reward a referent for being one you recognise.
proposals.rationale: R41 states '2013' outright, R29 turns on the Cubs' World Series, R54 names Ted Cruz, R20 names Trump, and R39 depends on Star Wars VII being imminent. Which night an entrant happened to play is upstream of the text and independent of their ability, yet it fixes the referent pool and leaves an obvious lexical trace, which can make a text-only model learn 'this era's nouns' rather than quality. Mixed, because a nightly topical contest genuinely rewards catching the moment, so the parent also has a legitimate quality path.
proposals.upstream_parent: the date of this contest within the programme's run and the state of the news cycle at submission time, which determines which referents were available and salient to every entrant that night

proposals.name: Headline Title-Case versus all-lowercase typing habit
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT of capitalisation applied to the joke span, ignoring hashtags and handles. 10 = every content word is capitalised, so the line reads as a headline or title. 5 = sentence case, first word only. 0 = entirely lowercase including proper-noun positions. Score orthography only. Do NOT judge whether the casing suits the joke, looks more polished, or reads as more confident.
proposals.rationale: Casing splits the slice while being orthogonal to content. Title-Cased entries include R08 'Need To Get Out', R14 'Deep-fried Chocolate-covered Hostess Twinkie', R44 'Raccoon Defeats Breathalyzer', R60 'We Were Always Great' and R16 'Proud Republican Tools'; all-lowercase entries include R24 "what's a dentist", R55 'automotive lawn art', R57 'barbecue flavored beard' and R56 'multiple COPS appearances'. Capitalisation is a keyboard habit. It changes nothing about the joke, it is trivially learnable from characters, and it is exactly the kind of typographic regularity a scorecard must never be allowed to import.

proposals.name: Taboo-lexicon density and self-masked profanity
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT of taboo vocabulary in the text: drug names, sexual terms, slurs, profanity, and asterisk- or symbol-masked versions of the same. 10 = multiple taboo tokens, or one carrying heavy charge, dominating the line. 5 = one mild taboo token. 0 = none. Count the vocabulary present, including masked forms, which score the same as unmasked. Do NOT judge whether the taboo material is funny, gratuitous, offensive, or well handled -- this is a lexical count, not a verdict on taste.
proposals.rationale: Taboo tokens are scattered across both directions of the disagreement -- R30 'Meth, Meth, Meth' and R36 'bullsh*t!' and R48 'Retarded' on one side, R11 'Rohypnol' and R04 'Post sex grits' on the other -- which is the signature of a lexical channel that a model can latch onto without tracking anything about comic construction. It is worth declaring precisely because it is easy to learn and points in inconsistent directions. Mixed, since edge is genuinely part of this venue's register and a blanket discount would remove real signal along with the spurious part.

proposals.name: Joke-span verbosity relative to the prompt's word budget
proposals.instruction: Score the EXTENT of length in the joke span only, excluding handle and hashtags. 10 = conspicuously long for a one-line contest entry -- a full clause with subordination, or well over the word count the prompt names. 5 = around the expected length. 0 = extremely terse, two or three words. Measure length alone. Do NOT judge whether the length is right for the joke, whether brevity is wittier, or whether the line earns its words.
proposals.rationale: Length varies widely and independently of construction here: R42 'What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?', R17 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation' and R32 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders' sit at the long end, while R38 'Judge Dread' and R34 'Overboard Politics' sit at the short end -- and both extremes appear among the card-favoured rows. Raw length is the classic free-riding proxy for any text scorer and must be declared before it can be mistaken for craft. I tag it mixed because economy under a stated word budget is a real property of a good entry, so discounting length wholesale would also erase a legitimate signal.

proposals.name: Persona-voice embodiment
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how fully the tweet reads as an authentic first-person statement spoken IN the voice of the contest persona (e.g., an actual redneck, an actual disillusioned citizen), with no signal that a comedian is standing outside the topic making a joke about it. A 10 is a flat, sincere-sounding in-character line with no pun apparatus or wink. A 0 is an obviously external, constructed joke (pun, reference, meta-remark) with no persona voice at all.
proposals.rationale: Rows R10 ('Git er done'), R14 ('That's my uncledad!'), R19 ('Father brother in-law'), R29 ('Y'all watch this'), R34 ('Up the Holler'), and R43 ('Tell you what.') are all dense_high_card_low and read as deadpan in-character statements. Contrast with card_high items like R01 ('Kill Bill of Rights') and R42 ('Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda'), which are clearly authored jokes ABOUT the topic rather than spoken from inside it.

proposals.name: Register clash on a closing/key term
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the degree to which the tweet builds a short list or phrase in one register (crude, vernacular, folksy) and then lands on a word from a sharply different register (formal, technical, elevated), producing tonal surprise. A 10 is a sharp, well-placed clash. A 0 is uniform register throughout with no tonal shift.
proposals.rationale: R51 ('Guns Nascar Beer Oligarchy') ends a redneck-coded list on the political-science term 'Oligarchy'; R44 ('We won't do Metric!') pairs a folksy refusal with the specific technical noun 'Metric.' Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards this clash while the scorecard does not.

proposals.name: Echo of a pre-existing idiom or catchphrase
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how clearly the tweet evokes and recontextualizes a specific, recognizable pre-existing saying, hymn line, bumper sticker, or meme phrase (not a movie title). A 10 clearly echoes a known phrase and repurposes it cleverly for the topic. A 0 has no such borrowed resonance -- entirely novel phrasing.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('Pass the ammunition') echoes the WWII-era line 'Praise the Lord and pass the ammunition'; R53 ('Dog: My Copilot') echoes the 'God is my co-pilot' bumper sticker. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting this borrowed-resonance humor is invisible to the scorecard.

proposals.name: Inventiveness of title-substitution (vs. rote swap)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how inventive a movie/show-title-based joke is. A 10 reworks the source title with a surprising, multi-layered mapping onto the new topic. A 0 is a single rote word-swap into an otherwise-unchanged famous title with minimal added wit.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('Kill Bill of Rights'), R30 ('Judge Dread'), R40 ('Dude, Where Are My Votes?'), and R57 ('12 Angry Men : The Contenders') are all card_high items following a near-identical 'famous title + one swapped element' template; several substitute only a single word with little added construction, which the scorecard appears to reward regardless of how thin the payoff is.

proposals.name: Absence of off-topic hashtag/content dilution
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for focus: a 10 has only the contest-relevant hashtag/handle and no extraneous tags, self-promotion, or unrelated content. A 0 is cluttered with hashtags or mentions unrelated to the contest topic that dilute the joke.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('Twerking Ever Since 2013 #PointsMe #July4thBirthday') and R18 ('Cubs Win the World Series ... #STLCards') and R54 ('Drunk Shriners Driving Small Cars ... #NeverForget') all carry extraneous, off-topic hashtags and are card_high, suggesting the scorecard does not penalize this dilution the way the dense model implicitly does.

proposals.name: Payoff independent of unseen linked media
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for whether the joke's full payoff is delivered by the text alone. A 10 is fully self-contained in the words. A 0 is essentially a caption/label whose actual comedic content lives in an attached link or photo the judge cannot see.
proposals.rationale: R22 ('automotive lawn art http://...') and R24 ('David Brent in porn flick ... https://...') and R54 (drunk-Shriners tweet with an attached link) are all card_high entries where the text is a thin label pointing at unseen media -- a property the scorecard cannot detect but which should count against text-only quality.

proposals.name: Engagement with the assigned topic vs. meta-commentary
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the joke is actually about the assigned theme versus about the contest/show/account itself. A 10 fully engages the assigned topic. A 0 is a joke about the meta-context (being on the show, tweeting from the wrong account, etc.) rather than the topic.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('"I saw myself on @midnight" #ScaryStoryIn5Words') and R26 ('Tweeted from the wrong account #ScaryStoryIn5Words') are both card_high and are jokes about the contest mechanics/show rather than about anything scary, suggesting the scorecard rewards cleverness even when it drifts off the assigned topic.

proposals.name: Double-entendre / simultaneous readings
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for whether the phrase supports at least two simultaneously valid, mutually reinforcing readings. A 10 has a genuine double meaning where both readings land. A 0 has exactly one flat, unambiguous reading.
proposals.rationale: R47 ('Proud Republican Tools') plays on 'tools' as both literal redneck tools and 'tools' meaning dupes/fools; R14 ('That's my uncledad!') forces two simultaneous kinship readings via portmanteau. Both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Implied backstory via repetition or escalating framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for whether the phrasing implies a larger untold history or sequence of events beyond the literal words, via repetition, ordinals, or escalating claims. A 10 strongly implies a bigger implicit narrative. A 0 is a single flat, isolated statement with no implied backstory.
proposals.rationale: R41 ('Meth, Meth, Meth') uses raw repetition to imply an ongoing pattern of behavior (dense_high); R55 ('Third tractor dui') uses the ordinal 'Third' to imply two prior unmentioned incidents (card_high) -- both rely on implication beyond the literal text, a mechanism neither model score alone seems to track consistently.

proposals.name: Grammatical/syntactic coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how clean and parseable the sentence construction is on a single read. A 10 is fully grammatical and immediately clear. A 0 is garbled enough that the reader must re-parse it to extract meaning.
proposals.rationale: R16 ('Me sleeping picture, live alone') is card_high but syntactically broken and hard to parse on first read, while dense_high items like R34 ('Up the Holler') and R20 ('Need To Get Out') are terse but grammatically clean.

proposals.name: Specificity of named political/cultural target
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for whether the tweet names a specific real person, party, policy, or slogan versus staying generic. A 10 names a precise target that sharpens the joke. A 0 stays vague/generic with no identifiable target.
proposals.rationale: R28 ('Democrats America's Retarded People') names a specific party; R60 ('We Were Always Great') subverts the specific 'Make America Great Again' slogan. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards precision the scorecard misses.

proposals.name: Concrete sensory imagery density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how vividly the phrase evokes a concrete, sensory (visual/tactile/gustatory) image in very few words. A 10 is densely concrete and vivid. A 0 is abstract or generic with no concrete image.
proposals.rationale: R37 ('Deep-fried Chocolate-covered Hostess Twinkie') piles up concrete, sensory nouns; R31 ('Road kill buffet') conjures a vivid single image. Both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Deliberate orthographic manipulation for double meaning
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for whether a spelling change, homophone swap, or unusual word choice is clearly deliberate and produces an added layer of meaning. A 10 is a clearly intentional alteration that adds a pun or ambiguity. A 0 is standard spelling throughout, or an error that adds no meaning.
proposals.rationale: R15 ('But we're we really?') uses a deliberate were/we're ambiguity to create an existential double-take (dense_high); R30 ('Judge Dread') swaps 'Dredd' for 'Dread' to fuse the movie reference with an emotional register (card_high) -- this mechanism shows up on both sides of the disagreement.

proposals.name: Thematic non-portability (topic-specific saturation)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how tightly the joke content is bound to THIS specific hashtag/theme, such that it would stop making sense under a different topic. A 10 could not be reused for another prompt without rewriting. A 0 is generic content that could be dropped into an unrelated hashtag almost unchanged.
proposals.rationale: R41 ('Meth, Meth, Meth') is tightly bound to the redneck-stereotype theme and dense_high; R52 ('Tastes great, less filling' under #AmericaIn4Words) card_high recycles a decades-old beer-ad slogan that is only loosely anchored to 'America' as a theme, suggesting the scorecard may reward recognizable borrowed phrasing even when its topical fit is thin.

proposals.name: Compression efficiency (payoff-per-word)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for whether every word in the tweet carries comedic weight, with nothing that could be cut without losing the joke. A 10 is maximally compressed with zero filler. A 0 has filler or redundant words that add length without adding payoff.
proposals.rationale: R10 ('Git er done') and R43 ('Tell you what.') are both extremely short, fully load-bearing, dense_high_card_low entries, suggesting the dense model rewards maximal compression that a criterion-by-criterion scorecard may not specifically credit.

proposals.name: Raw length (word/character count)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how long the tweet is in words/characters relative to the range seen in this slice, where 0 = among the shortest (a handful of words) and 10 = among the longest. This is a pure extent measure of length -- do NOT judge whether the length is good, appropriate, or well-used.
proposals.rationale: R28 ('Git er done') is extremely short while R47 ('What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?') is much longer; raw length is a mechanical surface count that could predict either model's score without being the actual source of comedic merit.

proposals.name: Hashtag capitalization style (camelCase vs lowercase)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how consistently the contest hashtag is written in CamelCase (each word capitalized) versus all-lowercase or irregular casing, where 0 = fully lowercase/irregular and 10 = fully and consistently CamelCased. Score only the typographic pattern -- do NOT judge whether this makes the tweet better.
proposals.rationale: R23 uses '#gopmovies' in lowercase while R08 uses '#GOPMovies' in CamelCase; this is a typing/formatting habit that a text classifier could pick up on as a proxy for something else (e.g. platform, device, or copy-paste source) rather than joke quality.

proposals.name: Terminal deadpan punctuation (trailing period/question mark)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the tweet ends its core phrase with an explicit period or question mark (as opposed to no terminal punctuation at all). 0 = no terminal punctuation, 10 = a clear terminal period or question mark closes the phrase. Score only presence of the punctuation mark -- do NOT judge whether the resulting tone is good.
proposals.rationale: R58 ('Tell you what.'), R59 ('Don't stop me now.'), and R15 ('But we're we really?') all close with explicit terminal punctuation and are all dense_high_card_low, raising the possibility that this purely typographic habit is being picked up as a stylistic tell rather than reflecting genuine joke quality.

proposals.name: Presence of an attached URL/link token
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the tweet's content is a bare URL token (e.g. 'http://...' or 'https://t.co/...'), where 0 = no URL present and 10 = the tweet is dominated by/built around a URL. Score only the presence and prominence of the URL string itself -- do NOT judge whether any linked photo/content (which you cannot see) is good.
proposals.rationale: R33 ('automotive lawn art http://...'), R12 ('David Brent in porn flick ... https://...'), R42 ('"I saw myself on @midnight" ... https://...'), and R01 ('Drunk Shriners Driving Small Cars ... https://...') all carry an attached link whose actual payoff is invisible to a text-only judge; the mere presence of a URL token is a formatting habit, not evidence of quality.

proposals.name: Extra community/leaderboard hashtag stacking
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how many hashtags beyond the single required contest hashtag are present (e.g. tracking hashtags, fan-community hashtags, personal-occasion hashtags), where 0 = only the required contest hashtag and 10 = multiple additional hashtags stacked on. Score only the count of extra hashtags -- do NOT judge whether they make the tweet better or worse.
proposals.rationale: R30 stacks '#PointsMe #July4thBirthday' onto the required tag, R43 adds '#STLCards', and R01 adds '#NeverForget' -- these look like fingerprints of a repeat-entrant's tracking/cross-posting habit rather than anything about the joke itself, though a practised regular entrant may also, separately, write genuinely sharper jokes (hence mixed).
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice/frequency in this format (e.g. regular entrants using third-party leaderboard-tracking tags, or cross-posting to other communities)

proposals.name: Meta-reference to the show/submission process itself
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet's content is about the act of being on the show, tweeting, or the contest mechanics itself (rather than about the assigned topic), where 0 = no such meta-reference and 10 = the tweet is entirely about the submission process/show. Score only presence of this meta-content -- do NOT judge whether it is clever.
proposals.rationale: R42 ('"I saw myself on @midnight"') and R05 ('Tweeted from the wrong account') are both jokes about the submission/broadcast process rather than the assigned topic; this pattern plausibly reflects an exposure-seeking motive that is orthogonal to (or even a distraction from) actually writing a good topical entry.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's motivation being exposure/validation from the show (e.g. wanting to be seen/favorited) rather than topical joke-writing

proposals.name: Named mainstream pop-culture franchise/brand density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how many specific, widely-recognized franchise, movie, TV-show, or brand names appear in the tweet (e.g. 'Star Wars', 'COPS', 'WalMart', 'Cubs'), where 0 = no such named franchise/brand and 10 = built entirely around one or more such names. Score only the presence/count of recognizable proper nouns -- do NOT judge whether the reference is used cleverly.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie'), R26 ('Star Wars VII: series finale'), and R14 ('multiple COPS appearances') all lean on instantly recognizable franchise names that could drive recognition-based favoriting regardless of how well-constructed the joke is; recognizability could also genuinely help a joke land, so this is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's recency/depth of mainstream media consumption and general audience recognizability, independent of joke construction

proposals.name: Named political figure/party proper-noun density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how many specific real political figures or party names are explicitly named in the tweet (e.g. 'Ted Cruz', 'Trump', 'Democrats'), where 0 = no named political figure/party and 10 = the tweet is built entirely around naming one or more. Score only the count of named political proper nouns -- do NOT judge whether the political content is funny or accurate.
proposals.rationale: R40 ('Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz'), R57 ('Half will vote Trump.'), and R35 ('Democrats America's Retarded People') all name specific political actors/parties; naming a real target could be independently rewarded by curators/audiences chasing engagement on hot-button topics, separate from the joke's craft (though precision of target could also be a genuine quality factor, hence mixed).
proposals.upstream_parent: topical alignment with the current news cycle and platform/curator appetite for politically-charged, high-engagement content

proposals.name: Taboo/shock subject-matter keyword presence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet's content centers on taboo or shock-value subject matter (illegal drugs, incest, sexual content, date-rape drugs, etc.), where 0 = no such content and 10 = the tweet's entire content is built around such subject matter. Score only the presence/intensity of the taboo subject matter as a topic -- do NOT judge whether it is used well.
proposals.rationale: R16 ('Family reunion Rohypnol'), R02 ('First Cousin lovin'''), and R45 ('That's my uncledad!') all foreground taboo subject matter; shock value alone can drive engagement separate from comedic craft, though taboo-violation is also a recognized comedic mechanism that could be genuinely funny, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/platform amplification of shock content (favoriting or sharing purely because content is shocking, independent of construction)

proposals.name: Convergent title-swap template fingerprint (late-stream bandwagon)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how closely the tweet follows an identical, already-common construction template within its contest (specifically: 'take one well-known title/phrase and swap in exactly one topical word/phrase, otherwise unchanged'), where 0 = a structurally unique construction not matching this template and 10 = a textbook instance of the exact same swap-one-word template seen repeatedly in the slice. Score only how closely the item matches this recurring template -- do NOT judge whether the specific swap is funny.
proposals.rationale: Within #GOPMovies, R08 ('Kill Bill of Rights'), R11 ('Judge Dread'), R24 ('Dude, Where Are My Votes?'), R25 ('Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda'), R29 ('12 Angry Men : The Contenders'), and R52 ('16 Angry Men (and one woman)') all instantiate the identical 'famous title, one word swapped' template, consistent with a wave of convergent, likely later-arriving entries riffing on a format that had already crystallized rather than each being an independently invented joke; a later, more considered entry could also genuinely be sharper, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (a late-arriving item written after the 'obvious' template for this prompt had already been established and imitated by earlier entrants, versus an early, idiosyncratic first response)

proposals.name: Constraint-Shaped Punchline
proposals.instruction: Score how actively the required word count creates the joke: 10 means the exact compact form is essential to the punchline, while 0 means the words merely happen to fit or fail to form a usable entry.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R07 turn three words into concise, line-like comic premises, unlike more list-like constructions such as R12.

proposals.name: Vivid Scene Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score the immediacy and specificity of the mental scene: 10 means the text instantly depicts a distinctive comic situation, while 0 means it remains abstract, generic, or image-poor.
proposals.rationale: R03, R24, and R57 supply unusually concrete objects and actions that can be visualized immediately.

proposals.name: Reversal Surprise
proposals.instruction: Score how sharply the line overturns an expected interpretation: 10 means a concise setup suddenly resolves in an unexpected way, while 0 means the statement is entirely predictable.
proposals.rationale: R08, R21, and R50 derive their premise from an unsettling or surprising reversal rather than a straightforward description.

proposals.name: Wordplay Precision
proposals.instruction: Score the cleanliness of linguistic transformation: 10 means a pun, blend, or substitution changes meaning precisely and is instantly recoverable, while 0 means there is no wordplay or it is strained and unclear.
proposals.rationale: R25, R26, R34, and R58 show different forms of compact blends, title alterations, and semantic substitutions.

proposals.name: Reference Transformation
proposals.instruction: Score how effectively a recognizable cultural reference is altered: 10 means the changed element creates a specific, integrated joke, while 0 means the reference is merely named or modified generically.
proposals.rationale: R14, R32, R42, and R46 all use familiar titles, but their comic value depends on how specifically the title is repurposed.

proposals.name: Cross-Domain Collision
proposals.instruction: Score the productive clash between unrelated domains: 10 means distant subjects combine into one coherent comic premise, while 0 means the elements are from one expected category or do not meaningfully connect.
proposals.rationale: R10, R26, and R52 combine politics, popular culture, consumer habits, and stereotyped objects into deliberately conflicting frames.

proposals.name: Implied Narrative
proposals.instruction: Score how much the wording implies a funny before-and-after sequence or escalating event: 10 means a tiny line suggests a whole story, while 0 means it is only a static label or list.
proposals.rationale: R07, R23, and R57 imply imminent action, consequences, or an unseen backstory beyond their literal words.

proposals.name: Character Voice Authenticity
proposals.instruction: Score how naturally the line sounds like a specific person speaking: 10 means it has idiomatic, character-revealing voice, while 0 means it sounds mechanically assembled, unnatural, or interchangeable.
proposals.rationale: R13, R23, R44, and R60 use strongly spoken idioms whose effect depends on believable comic voice.

proposals.name: Cadence And Sonic Snap
proposals.instruction: Score the line's spoken rhythm and sound pattern: 10 means repetition, stress, alliteration, or cadence makes it especially punchy aloud, while 0 means it is flat, clumsy, or sonically forgettable.
proposals.rationale: R22 uses emphatic repetition, R35 uses compact rhythmic phrasing, and R42 gains force from its balanced title-like cadence.

proposals.name: Novel Recombination
proposals.instruction: Score the originality of the element combination while preserving intelligibility: 10 means the pairing feels fresh yet immediately understandable, while 0 means it is a stock template or random incoherence.
proposals.rationale: R03, R55, and R57 pair familiar ideas in notably uncommon combinations without requiring a long explanation.

proposals.name: Specific Satirical Target
proposals.instruction: Score the precision of the target: 10 means the line points at a concrete person, institution, behavior, or practice with a compressed angle, while 0 means it expresses only a vague attitude or slogan.
proposals.rationale: R10 targets government corruption, R20 names a specific political figure, and R52 compresses several identifiable American institutions and habits.

proposals.name: Double-Reading Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score whether one wording supports two simultaneous coherent interpretations: 10 means both readings reinforce the joke, while 0 means the line has only one literal meaning and no semantic tension.
proposals.rationale: R16, R49, and R58 rely on words that can be read both literally and figuratively, producing extra meaning from minimal text.

proposals.name: Interpretive Tension
proposals.instruction: Score the tension between the line's surface claim and an implied contradiction or question: 10 means it invites a second thought that deepens the joke, while 0 means it simply asserts the expected premise.
proposals.rationale: R04, R31, R48, and R54 create friction between patriotic language and doubt, dissatisfaction, or self-questioning.

proposals.name: Self-Contained Clarity
proposals.instruction: Score how completely the joke works from the tweet and hashtag alone: 10 means it is clear without links, explanation, or obscure missing context, while 0 means it is dependent on unavailable material or is grammatically opaque.
proposals.rationale: R06, R19, and R55 include links or contextual dependencies that compete with the text's ability to stand on its own.

proposals.name: Nonliteral Hashtag Fit
proposals.instruction: Score how creatively the line uses the prompt's frame: 10 means it feels native to the hashtag while adding an unexpected angle, while 0 means it is merely a literal stereotype, generic reference, or pasted-in slogan.
proposals.rationale: R12, R39, and R45 demonstrate the difference between directly naming expected material and developing a more distinctive relationship to the hashtag.

proposals.name: Contest-shell boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the tweet consists of contest-shell boilerplate such as @midnight, the contest hashtag, and their framing or placement. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R08 place the handle and hashtag before the entry, while R01 and R06 place them after it. This shell can proxy copy-paste workflow or submission habits and affect processing independently of entry merit.

proposals.name: Promotion and link residue
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the tweet contains outward-promotion or attachment residue, such as URLs, extra promotional hashtags, or media-directed wording. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R18 and R32 append URLs, while R33 adds promotional hashtags and R52 combines an extra hashtag with a URL. These traces can proxy promotion habits or media-sharing processes and alter attention independently of the one-line wording.

proposals.name: Vernacular spelling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the wording uses regionally marked vernacular, eye-dialect, or nonstandard contractions and spellings. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R07 uses Y'all watch this, R15 uses Holler, and R56 uses Git er done; R34 and R47 add marked spellings such as Readin's and lovin'. These cues can proxy regional identity and format practice, which may affect reception and also influence actual construction.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's regional vernacular and practice in the format

proposals.name: Rushed-editing residue
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the wording shows rushed-editing residue, including agreement errors, typos, malformed syntax, or visible correction attempts. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R14 contains a repeated or incorrect we are construction, R21 has an awkward kinship phrase, and R25 compresses a sentence into telegraphic wording. Such residue can proxy haste, phone entry, or limited editing and affect readability apart from the underlying concept.

proposals.name: Explanatory add-ons
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the tweet adds explanatory scaffolding such as parentheses, glosses, subtitles, or clarifying appositives. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R27 supplies a parenthetical expansion, R38 adds a subtitle after a colon, and R48 adds a parenthetical qualification. This can proxy clarification habits, editing, or assistance and change interpretation without being a standalone merit property.

proposals.name: Taboo-reference load
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the tweet uses profane, stigmatized, graphic, or socially transgressive references. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R20, R22, R44, and R49 use profane or taboo references, while R55 and R60 use stigmatized relationship or drug language. Such cues can trigger audience-norm or moderation effects independently of craft; taboo presence is not itself a quality judgment.

proposals.name: Franchise-title anchoring
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the wording depends on named films, franchises, characters, or other recognizable entertainment titles. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R03 names Star Wars, R16 invokes Judge Dread, and R39 names Jar Jar Binks; R10 and R54 likewise use recognizable film-title forms. Familiarity can affect comprehension and attention, while title anchoring is only a subject-matter fingerprint.

proposals.name: Current-affairs anchoring
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the wording depends on current political figures, parties, institutions, or partisan controversies. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R17, R35, and R57 use political institutions, ideology, or a prominent public figure, while R13 uses a policy-domain reference. Such wording can proxy news-cycle timing and audience alignment, affecting attention independently of construction.
proposals.upstream_parent: news-cycle timing and audience faction alignment

proposals.name: Stream-position fingerprint
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the wording carries a stream-position cue, such as a bare canonical completion versus an elaborated follow-on riff that assumes an obvious baseline. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether the implied position is good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R37 read like compact canonical prompt completions, whereas R38 and R48 use subtitle or qualification structures that can read as follow-on riffs. This contrast can proxy composition within a crowded stream or awareness of prior entries.

proposals.name: Hashtag casing variance
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the contest hashtag shows unusual capitalization, spelling, or casing relative to the contest form displayed with the item. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether the variation is correct, good, funny, or desirable.
proposals.rationale: R17 uses lower-case #gopmovies, R38 uses all-caps #GOPMOVIES, and R45 uses mixed-case #GOPMovies. This variance can proxy client choice, copying behavior, or formatting practice and influence parsing without describing entry merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission client, copy-paste behavior, or author formatting practice

proposals.name: Unexpected semantic collision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when two familiar ideas collide in a surprising, instantly graspable way; score 0 when the ideas merely coexist without a comic connection.
proposals.rationale: The collision in R13 and R44 creates a sharper conceptual jolt than straightforward topical labeling.

proposals.name: Premise-to-punchline linkage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every major word contributes to one coherent comic reinterpretation; score 0 when the wording is a disconnected list or unrelated phrase.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R21 form unified satirical statements, unlike list-like constructions such as R46.

proposals.name: Layered wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording supports two simultaneous meanings that reinforce each other; score 0 when it has only one literal reading.
proposals.rationale: The kinship inventions in R06 and R52 reward semantic layering, as does the double meaning in R23.

proposals.name: Familiar-frame novelty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar phrase is bent into a genuinely new comic meaning; score 0 when it simply repeats a stock expression unchanged.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R27 rely on familiar language, while R18 and R35 illustrate how recognizable wording can remain comparatively untransformed.

proposals.name: Implicit scene completion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a short line makes the reader instantly imagine a specific comic scene or preceding event; score 0 when it supplies no actionable situation beyond a fragment.
proposals.rationale: R12 and R17 evoke recognizable scenes through compressed dialogue, whereas R33 offers mostly an isolated phrase.

proposals.name: Distinctive comic voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when diction and phrasing create a vivid, specific speaker or persona; score 0 when the wording could belong to anyone and carries no voice.
proposals.rationale: R31 and R46 strongly establish a regional persona, while R36 uses a more generic topical label.

proposals.name: Beyond-stereotype specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke uses a concrete, unusual behavior or detail rather than merely listing expected stereotypes; score 0 when it is an interchangeable stereotype inventory.
proposals.rationale: R25 and R37 turn redneck imagery into specific situations, contrasting with the token lists in R46 and R55.

proposals.name: Absurd escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary premise escalates to a vivid, disproportionate comic consequence; score 0 when nothing is heightened beyond the initial premise.
proposals.rationale: R25 and R41 intensify their premises through grotesque excess, while R32 mainly states an outrageous situation without a developed escalation.

proposals.name: Punchline finality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the ending supplies a clear, satisfying comic landing; score 0 when the line feels like an unfinished setup or stops before its point.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R21 end on decisive turns, whereas R17 and R42 feel more dependent on imagined continuation.

proposals.name: Semantic economy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when nearly every content word adds distinct comic information; score 0 when the joke contains padding, repetition, or arbitrary wording.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R44 pack several ideas into compact lines, while R20 and R40 spend words without an equally concentrated payoff.

proposals.name: Phonetic snap
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when rhythm, stress, repetition, or sound pattern makes the line naturally satisfying to say; score 0 when its phrasing is awkward or sonically flat.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R41 gain force from cadence and repetition, while R49 illustrates phrasing whose sound and grammar interrupt the joke.

proposals.name: Reference recontextualization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a movie, celebrity, or cultural reference is altered to make a sharp comment about the prompt; score 0 when a reference is pasted in with only superficial substitution.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R15 demonstrate elaborate title transformations, while R01 and R18 mainly append familiar references to a generic premise.

proposals.name: Concrete topical mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the hashtag topic is connected to a concrete behavior, contradiction, or institution; score 0 when the line merely includes topical keywords or labels.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R44 connect politics to concrete mechanisms, whereas R10 and R43 rely more heavily on broad associative wording.

proposals.name: Productive ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when ambiguity invites a second comic interpretation while remaining understandable; score 0 when ambiguity is accidental, confusing, or merely ungrammatical.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R21 use uncertainty as a rhetorical device, while R33 and R49 risk leaving the reader unsure what the sentence means.

proposals.name: Self-contained readability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke is fully understandable from the text alone without external media or missing context; score 0 when it requires a link, image, or substantial reconstruction.
proposals.rationale: R20 and R58 explicitly lean on linked or quoted context, while R27 and R44 communicate their comic premise independently.

proposals.name: Contest-wrapper clutter
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much boilerplate account, hashtag, date, or link material surrounds the entry text; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Submission wrappers vary in density and placement, as seen in R01 and R02, and may reflect posting conventions rather than comic construction.

proposals.name: Typography irregularity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much nonstandard capitalization, spacing, punctuation, apostrophe use, quotation, or parenthetical formatting appears; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Visible seams occur in R16, R27, and R54; such typography can attract attention or signal informality without describing comic quality.

proposals.name: External-media cue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains URLs, quoted media, or explicit references to attached external content; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: External-content traces appear in R02, R17, R33, and R53, potentially changing audience engagement because of posting mechanics rather than the one-line idea.

proposals.name: Proper-noun load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry uses named people, brands, franchises, institutions, or other recognizable proper nouns; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: R04, R08, and R13 rely heavily on recognizable names or titles; familiarity can shape audience response and can also overlap with genuine topical aptness.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience familiarity and contemporary topic salience

proposals.name: Identity-polarization cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much explicit partisan, religious, regional, or culture-war identity language appears; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: R21, R35, R46, and R56 contain strong identity signals that may activate audience alignment or opposition independently of the line's construction.

proposals.name: Format-fluency idiom
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry uses stock catchphrases, community vernacular, or familiar formulaic speech associated with this contest format; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Formulaic vernacular is prominent in R24, R48, and R57; practiced entrants may use such language more often, while practice may also genuinely improve writing.

proposals.name: Insider self-reference
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry references the show, host, contest mechanics, account identity, or participation history beyond required metadata; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: R07, R49, and R53 include participation or show-awareness cues that may influence perceived belonging or familiarity without being intrinsic to comic quality.

proposals.name: Revision residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text shows visible typo residue, grammar correction, explanatory glosses, or awkward seams suggesting uneven drafting; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: R16, R54, and R58 show different kinds of drafting residue; submission or editing conditions can affect reception and can also alter the underlying line itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: rushed submission or uneven editing assistance

proposals.name: Canonical first-association
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the wording resembles an immediate, stereotyped, literal first completion of the prompt; judge presence only, not whether that completion is good.
proposals.rationale: R24, R25, and R39 use highly canonical prompt-associated wording; such phrasing may signal early or crowded-stream placement rather than quality.

proposals.name: Recency-marker load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry contains explicit dates, sequels, current events, live results, or other time-sensitive markers; judge presence only, not whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: R01, R10, and R30 contain explicit temporal or then-current references; timing can alter audience familiarity and may sometimes also contribute genuinely to prompt fit.
